tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (test.cpp times the real std::lower_bound against sb_lower_bound), and compiler and flags are stated (g++-10/clang++-10 -std=c++20 -O2 -march=haswell). The only hardware given is 'an intel i7 kaby lake', a CPU generation with no model/SKU, so tier A is not met; first-party partial methodology is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Primitive types, average ns/call: with clang++-10 -mllvm -x86-cmov-converter=false, sb_lower_bound 33.24 vs std::lower_bound 61.30 (~1.84x, derived from page data), geometric mean 19.81 vs 39.17. Without that flag it is roughly parity: gcc 77.22 vs 80.68, clang 80.06 vs 78.66 (sb slower). 8-byte strings: sb_lower_bound slightly slower in every column (gcc 165.66 vs 160.01, clang 162.68 vs 157.71, clang -cmov 164.71 vs 156.06). The article headline says '2x faster'. A later update reports ~2.3x (std::lower_bound ~161 ns vs the prefetching variant sbpm_lower_bound ~71 ns) on arrays up to ~128M entries.
corrections.caveats: MIT-licensed via LICENSES/MIT.txt and SPDX headers in every file, but GitHub's API does not detect it. The ~1.8x win needs clang with -mllvm -x86-cmov-converter=false. With gcc or default clang it is about as fast as std::lower_bound, and it is slightly slower for 8-byte string keys. Author's own benchmark on one unspecified Kaby Lake i7. Small project (24 stars), last pushed July 2023.

notes: The record said no license, but LICENSES/MIT.txt plus SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT headers exist, and the article says 'MIT license'. The record also dropped the clang -cmov-converter=false condition from the 2x headline. libc++ was never actually tested: clang++-10 runs had no -stdlib=libc++ flag, and the article mentions libc++ only as a source reference.

tier_reason: Code is public (binary_search.c, monobound_bsearch.c benchmarks bsearch from stdlib.h), and the compiler and flags are stated (GCC 7.5.0, gcc -O3, WSL 2). The CPU is only 'Intel i3 quad-core processor' with no model, so tier A is not met: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: monobound binary search 'executes two to four times faster than the standard binary search on arrays smaller than 1 million 32 bit integers' and is 'up to 60% faster than the standard binary search when comparing 32 bit integers'. Both compare against the repo's own standard_binary_search, not bsearch. Boundless binary search gain 'should be around 20% when comparing 32 bit integers'. Against libc bsearch() with the same comparator-callback interface (monobound_bsearch.c): 0.000136 vs 0.000202 s at 10 elements, 0.000265 vs 0.000623 s at 1000, 0.002641 vs 0.003784 s at 10M, about 1.4-2.35x faster across sizes (derived from page data).

notes: The record misattributed the README's 'up to 60% faster' claim to bsearch(). That claim is vs the textbook standard binary search. The real bsearch table shows ~1.4-2.35x. Metadata verified: Unlicense, 683 stars, 44 forks, last commit 2025-06-20 (stale).

tier_reason: Public code: 2026/04/26/benchmark/benchmarks/simple.cpp times std::binary_search(arr.begin(), arr.end(), k) and std::find against simd_quad. CMakeLists.txt forces a Release build (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG, C++23, no -march). Compilers are named (GCC, Apple LLVM; versions unstated), and one machine is an exact chip (Apple M4), so A holds. The Intel machine is only 'Emerald Rapids'.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Results are charts only. Post: 'in all instances, SIMD Quad is faster than the binary search' (std::binary_search). Intel Emerald Rapids/GCC: 'more than twice as fast as the binary search on the warm cache. The benefits are lesser on the cold cache.' Apple M4/Apple LLVM: 'it is with the cold cache that the SIMD Quad is more than twice as fast, whereas the benefits are more marginal on the warm cache.' The quad step over plain SIMD binary 'has little effect on the Apple platform, but it is a decent optimization on the Intel platform for large arrays in the cold case.'
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC (Intel Emerald Rapids run) and Apple LLVM (Apple M4 run), versions not stated. The benchmark's CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG) with C++23 and no -march flags. simple.cpp times std::binary_search(arr.begin(), arr.end(), k) and std::find(arr.begin(), arr.end(), k) != arr.end().
corrections.caveats: Single-author blog benchmark, not a packaged library. The implementation is a ~20-line function in the post's appendix and in 2026/04/26/benchmark/benchmarks/simple.cpp. The monorepo has no LICENSE file. Results are charts without numeric tables. The >2x gain holds only for warm cache on Intel and cold cache on Apple M4; the other cache mode gives smaller gains. Only two machines tested, and the Intel one is identified only as Emerald Rapids.

notes: The record overstated the claim as >2x 'in every tested configuration'. The post says >2x only for Intel-warm and Apple-cold, with smaller gains otherwise. It also says the quad step barely helps on Apple. No numeric values appear in the post text (charts only), so numbers_found_on_page=false for the quoted qualitative claims. last_commit 2026-04-27 is the benchmark directory's commit; the repo's latest commit is 2026-09-24.

tier_reason: The results file shows std::strstr 0.662049 s vs AVX2 (generic) 0.363694 s (three runs, identical checksums). The code is public (src/speedup.cpp, Makefile speedup_avx2 target with -O3 -mavx2). The compiler (GCC 5.4.1) and CPU (i7-6700) are stated in the result filename.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -I. -DHAVE_SSE_INSTRUCTIONS -mavx2 -DHAVE_AVX2_INSTRUCTIONS -DNDEBUG (current Makefile speedup_avx2 target). GCC 5.4.1 for the cited result (from the result filename). results/ also has GCC 4.8.4-7.4.0 and Clang 3.8.0 runs on other CPUs.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) for the cited number. results/ also covers ARMv7, ARMv8 (Clang 3.8.0), AMD Bulldozer FX-8510, Intel Haswell i7-4770, Knights Landing 7210, Skylake i9-7900, Cascade Lake Xeon Gold 5217, and Westmere M540.
corrections.caveats: Companion sample code for a 2016-era article on SIMD substring search. Last commit January 2022 (abandoned). The ~1.8x figure is for one kernel/CPU pairing, and results vary widely by kernel and machine in results/. The 'std::strstr' row is the unqualified C strstr (glibc on the GCC/Linux runs), not the generic std::search. speedup.cpp deliberately skips std::string::find on GCC builds ('proven to be utterly slow'), so it has no numbers on x86.

notes: Numbers match the result file exactly. libc++ is not evidenced: all x86 runs are GCC, and the baseline is glibc strstr. Metadata verified: BSD-2-Clause, 266 stars, last commit 2022-01-04, not archived.

tier_reason: The README states 'about 45 GB/s on an Apple M-series core, 30x the platform memmem'. It gives no exact CPU model, compiler version, or results table for that figure. The README says benchmark numbers should be run on your own machine. First-party numbers with partial methodology: C.

corrections.baseline: memmem (platform libc; the headline figure is on an Apple M-series core)
corrections.caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (reference usability only). The '45 GB/s, 30x memmem' figure names only an 'Apple M-series core', and the README says benchmark numbers should be measured on your own machine. benchmark/README.md notes Apple's libc memmem 'uses a much simpler scan and lands well behind strstr', so 30x is against a weak baseline. The benchmark driver includes strstr and std::search variants, but no numbers against them are published. Requires AVX-512F+BW on x86-64 (no runtime dispatch) or NEON.

notes: The headline claim is quoted correctly. The baseline is memmem, a POSIX/GNU extension rather than ISO C, and Apple's implementation is weak per the repo's own docs. Metadata verified: no license, 9 stars, last commit 2026-09-21, not a fork.
